**DOM**: ready for a specified operation, **excluding all fuel and traffic load**; includes crew + baggage, catering and removable passenger service equipment, potable water and lavatory chemicals.
**Traffic load** (payload): the revenue-earning load.
**Ramp mass** = DOM + usable fuel + traffic load. **Take-off mass** = ramp mass - start & taxi fuel.
**Max traffic load** = MSTOM - DOM - take-off fuel.
**MZFM**: max permissible mass with no usable fuel.
**RATOM/MATOM** = lesser of MSTOM or performance-limited TOM. **RLM/MALM** = lesser of MLM or performance-limited LM.
**Payload** is the lowest of three limits: RTOW-based, MLW + flight fuel, MZFW + FOB.

**Start & taxi**: APU/engine start and taxi to the threshold. **Trip**: take-off run, climb, cruise, descent, arrival, approach and landing. **Contingency**: % of trip for unforeseen events. **Alternate**: missed approach at destination -> alternate and landing. **Final reserve**: 45 min piston / 30 min jet. **Additional**: only if the above are insufficient.

cards.q: How do you calculate CG?
cards.a: CG = total moment / total mass, where moment = mass x arm from the datum. Nose-up moments positive.

cards.q: What are datum and balance arm?
cards.a: Datum: reference point on the longitudinal axis from which arms are measured. Balance arm: distance from datum to the CG of a mass.

cards.q: Explain BEM, DOM, ramp mass, take-off mass.
cards.a: BEM: aircraft + basic equipment + unusable fuel/oil. DOM: ready for operation excluding fuel and traffic load (crew, catering, water). Ramp = DOM + fuel + traffic load. Take-off mass = ramp - start/taxi fuel.

cards.q: MZFM?
cards.a: Maximum permissible mass of the aeroplane with no usable fuel.

cards.q: How do you find max traffic load?
cards.a: MSTOM - DOM - take-off fuel.

cards.q: How do you calculate payload?
cards.a: Take the lowest of: RTOW, MLW + flight fuel, MZFW + FOB; then subtract OM/FOB to get the allowed payload.

notes.b:
**TORA**: take-off run available. **TODA** = TORA + clearway (cannot exceed 1.5 x TORA). **ASDA** = TORA + stopway. **LDA** = length of runway from threshold to threshold available for landing.
**Balanced field**: ASDA = TODA (a runway with no stopway or clearway is balanced).
**Clearway**: area beyond the runway, **at least 152 m (500 ft) wide**, centred on the extended centreline, under airport authority control; a plane sloping up at **not more than 1.25%** with no obstacle through it. Purpose: ensure aircraft doesn't hit obstacles after leaving the runway.
**Stopway**: area beyond the take-off run, at least as wide as the runway, able to support the aeroplane in an abort without structural damage.

**Critical engine**: the engine whose failure most adversely affects performance or handling.
**Damp runway**: not dry, but moisture doesn't give a shiny appearance.
**Hydroplaning speed**: speed at which the wheel is lifted off by a depth of water and directional control through it is impossible.
**Pressure altitude**: altitude above the 1013.25 hPa level.
**Service ceiling**: pressure altitude where rate of climb falls to a specified value (~300 ft/min). **Absolute ceiling**: ROC = 0. Both decrease with higher mass and temperature.
**ACN vs PCN**: ACN (aircraft) must not exceed PCN (pavement). A 10% exceedance is generally acceptable on good pavement; occasional use with ACN up to 50% above PCN may be permitted.
**Gross performance**: average fleet performance if well maintained and flown per manual. **Net performance**: gross, diminished for contingencies (pilot technique, below-average performance). **Measured performance**: achieved by manufacturer under test conditions with new aircraft and test pilots.
**En-route phase**: from 1500 ft above take-off surface to 1000 ft above landing aerodrome (Class B) or 1500 ft (Class A).
**Flat-rated engine**: thrust capped at a maximum even though the engine could produce more; below the flat rating cut-off (typically ISA +15 C) thrust isn't affected by temperature.
**Take-off mass**: mass including everything at the start of take-off run.
**Performance limited mass**: set by field length, climb, tyre speed, brake energy. **Regulated TOM**: the lower of performance-limited and max structural mass.

cards.q: Define TORA, TODA, ASDA, LDA.
cards.a: TORA: take-off run available. TODA: TORA + clearway (max 1.5 x TORA). ASDA: TORA + stopway. LDA: runway length available for landing, threshold to threshold.

cards.q: What is a balanced field?
cards.a: ASDA = TODA (e.g. a runway without stopway or clearway).

cards.q: Clearway vs stopway?
cards.a: Clearway: at least 152 m wide area beyond runway under authority control, slope not more than 1.25%, free of obstacles; lets aircraft climb out. Stopway: area at least as wide as runway able to support an aborted take-off without damage.

cards.q: Gross vs net vs measured performance?
cards.a: Gross: average fleet performance flown per manual. Net: gross reduced for contingencies. Measured: test-condition performance by test pilots on new aircraft.

cards.q: Service ceiling vs absolute ceiling?
cards.a: Service ceiling: rate of climb falls to a specified value (~300 ft/min). Absolute: rate of climb is zero.

cards.q: ACN and PCN?
cards.a: ACN is aircraft load on pavement; PCN is pavement strength. Operation allowed if ACN <= PCN; 10% over is generally acceptable on good pavement.

cards.q: What is a flat-rated engine?
cards.a: Thrust limited to a maximum even though engine can produce more; below flat-rating temperature (~ISA +15) thrust unaffected by temperature.

notes.t: The story of a take-off in V speeds
notes.b: Accelerating down the runway: **VMCG** (can I control it on the ground if an engine dies?) -> **VEF** (engine fails here) -> **V1** (decision) -> **VR** (rotate) -> **VMU/VLOF** (lift-off) -> **V2** (safety speed by 35 ft) -> **V3** (all-engine climb speed).

**VMCG**: minimum speed on the ground at which the take-off can safely continue when the critical engine suddenly fails with the rest at take-off thrust. Only the rudder is used (ailerons would bank the wing into the ground; no nosewheel steering). Depends on thrust, i.e. air density: **density up = VMCG up**.
**VMCA/VMC**: minimum control speed in the air, max **5 deg bank**, critical engine failed suddenly, others at take-off thrust. **VMCL**: landing approach version with a wing engine inoperative.
**VEF**: CAS at which the critical engine is assumed to fail; never less than VMCG.
**V1**: the maximum speed at which the first action must be taken to stop within the ASDA (**VSTOP**), and the minimum speed after engine failure at which the take-off can be continued within TODA (**VGO**).
Engine failure **before V1 -> abort**. **After V1 -> continue**.
V1 rules: not less than VEF + speed gained until the pilot reacts; not more than VR; not more than VMBE; not less than VMCG.
**VMBE**: max brake energy speed - the max ground speed from which the brakes can safely stop. Heavier mass reduces it; also affected by pressure altitude, temperature, slope, wind.
**VMU**: minimum unstick speed. **VLOF**: speed at which main wheels leave the ground (should be faster than VMU).
**VR**: pilot begins rotation. Not less than V1, 1.05 VMC, or a speed allowing V2 by 35 ft. Increasing mass increases VR; flaps down decreases VR; density down increases VR.
**V2**: take-off safety speed, target one-engine-out speed, reached by 35 ft. Must exceed stall and VMC. After engine failure, fly **V2 until 400 ft**.
**V3**: steady initial climb speed with all engines.
**VLE** = max speed with gear extended. **VLO** = max speed to operate the gear. **VREF** = speed at landing screen height.

- Mass up -> V1 up.
- Flap angle up -> V1 down.
- Density down -> V1 up.
- Downslope -> V1 down; upslope -> V1 up.
- Tailwind -> V1 down; headwind -> V1 up.
Early rotation (at low speed): lift-off still happens at VLOF but with more drag while rotated, so a longer distance to lift-off.

cards.q: What is V1?
cards.a: Decision speed: max speed at which the first stopping action must be taken to stop within the ASDA (VSTOP), and the min speed after engine failure from which take-off can be continued within TODA (VGO). Failure before V1 abort; after V1 continue.

cards.q: What limits V1?
cards.a: Not less than VEF + gain until reaction, not less than VMCG, not more than VR, not more than VMBE.
cards.tip: V1 lives in a sandwich: VMCG below, VMBE (and VR) above.

cards.q: What affects V1?
cards.a: Mass up -> up; flaps up (more flap) -> down; density down -> up; downslope -> down; tailwind -> down.

cards.q: What is VMCG and why use the rudder only?
cards.a: Min ground control speed when critical engine fails at take-off thrust. Ailerons cannot be used on the ground (would bank into the ground), so only rudder. Higher density = more thrust = higher VMCG.

cards.q: VR rules?
cards.a: Not less than V1, 1.05 VMC, or a speed that allows V2 by 35 ft. Mass up -> VR up; flap up -> VR down; density down -> VR up.

cards.q: What is V2 and how long do you fly it after engine failure?
cards.a: Take-off safety speed with one engine inoperative, reached by the screen height; above stall and VMC; fly V2 until 400 ft.

cards.q: VMU vs VLOF?
cards.a: VMU: slowest CAS where aeroplane can safely lift off and continue. VLOF: actual speed when main wheels leave the runway, should be above VMU.

cards.q: What is VMBE?
cards.a: Maximum brake energy speed - max speed from which the brakes can safely stop the aeroplane; V1 may not exceed it.

notes.b:
From **35 ft** (15 ft for a contaminated runway) to **1500 ft** above the take-off surface. Four segments:
**Segment 1**: starts at 35 ft at V2, one engine out; ends **gear up and locked**. Gradient must be positive.
**Segment 2**: gear up -> climb at not less than V2 to **400 ft**. **Most severe requirement: 2.4%** (twin jet).
**Segment 3**: at/above 400 ft: **acceleration and flap retraction** from V2 to zero-flap speed and then to final take-off speed (= best one-engine-out angle of climb).
**Segment 4**: flaps up, final segment speed, **maximum continuous thrust**; climb to 1500 ft; gradient not less than **1.2%**.

Turns not below half the wingspan or 50 ft (whichever is greater). Bank limit: **15 deg up to 400 ft**, **25 deg above 400 ft**.
Net take-off flight path clears obstacles by **35 ft** vertically; if a turn of more than 15 deg is needed, **50 ft**.
**Climb limit mass** (WAT/MAT limit): max mass that meets the minimum climb performance - the most severe requirement is **2.4%**.

Steady climb: **T = D + W sin(theta)** -> **sin(theta) = (T - D)/W**. Climb gradient = height gained / distance = tan(angle).
**Rate of climb** = (power available - power required)/W; max when excess power is greatest = **Vy**.

Landing distance starts at **50 ft** screen height (fixed for all classes; take-off screen is 35 ft for class A, 50 ft for class B) and ends at a complete stop. Must reach **VREF** by the screen.
Two parts: **airborne section** (50 ft to main wheel touchdown, ~1000 ft) and **ground roll**. Landing distance formula (simplified): **d = V^2 / 2a**.

cards.q: Explain the four take-off climb segments.
cards.a: Seg 1: 35 ft at V2 until gear up. Seg 2: gear up to 400 ft at V2, min gradient 2.4% (twin jet). Seg 3: level acceleration and flap retraction to final take-off speed. Seg 4: max continuous thrust to 1500 ft, gradient not less than 1.2%.

cards.q: Bank limits on take-off flight path?
cards.a: No turns below half wingspan or 50 ft; 15 deg bank up to 400 ft; 25 deg above 400 ft.

cards.q: Obstacle clearance on net take-off path?
cards.a: 35 ft vertical; 50 ft if turn of more than 15 deg.

cards.q: What is the climb limit mass?
cards.a: Max mass at which the aeroplane meets the minimum (most severe) climb gradient requirement, 2.4%. Also called WAT/MAT limit.

cards.q: Which speed gives max rate of climb?
cards.a: Vy, where excess power is greatest.

cards.q: Where does the landing distance start?
cards.a: 50 ft above threshold (landing screen height) until the aeroplane stops; airborne section ~1000 ft plus ground roll.

notes.b:
A precision runway approach aid using **two radio beams** giving horizontal AND vertical guidance. Three ground parts:
- **Localiser (LLZ)**: **VHF**, about **300 m beyond** the upwind (far) end of the runway.
- **Glide path (GP)**: **UHF**, frequency-paired with the localiser; located ~300 m in from threshold and ~200 m off the runway edge, abeam the touchdown point.
- **Marker beacons**: all **75 MHz**: outer, middle, possibly inner marker. They let you cross-check height vs range/timing.

Localiser **108.0-111.975 MHz** (odd first decimal digit). Glidepath **329.15-335 MHz**. Markers **75 MHz**.
**DME paired with ILS**: supplements or replaces markers; zero-referenced to the ILS threshold; protected only inside the localiser service area up to **25 000 ft**.
4-letter Morse at 7 groups/min; first letter usually **I**. Suppressed if the ILS is unserviceable or withdrawn; removed or replaced by continuous tone during maintenance/test.

The localiser makes **two overlapping lobes** on a single VHF frequency, modulated differently (90 Hz and 150 Hz). Modulation depth increases away from centreline. **DDM = 0** is the centreline.
**False glideslopes**: other paths in the vertical plane with DDM zero; caused by metallic structures at the transmitter, ground reflections, aerial height. First false glideslope at about **twice the glide path angle (6 deg for a 3 deg GP)**; always **above** the true glide path, so not dangerous.
**ILS reference datum**: point ~**50 ft** above the intersection of centreline and threshold through which the glidepath passes. PAPI gives visual glidepath matching the ILS, designed for mean eye height of pilot (MEHT).

Localiser full-scale deflection: **2.5 deg** each side = **0.5 deg per dot**.
Glide path full-scale: **0.7 deg** = **0.14 deg per dot**. Max safe deviation below glideslope: half-scale = **2.5 dots fly up** (the EGPWS mode 5B hard alert).

cards.q: What are the components of ILS and their bands?
cards.a: Localiser (VHF, 108-111.975 MHz, ~300 m beyond upwind end), glide path (UHF, 329.15-335 MHz, ~300 m in from threshold and 200 m offset), markers (75 MHz).

cards.q: How do you know a localiser frequency?
cards.a: 108.0-111.975 MHz with an ODD first decimal digit (e.g. 109.1).

cards.q: How does the localiser work?
cards.a: Two overlapping lobes on one VHF frequency, modulated differently; modulation depth rises away from the centreline; DDM zero = centreline.

cards.q: What are false glideslopes?
cards.a: Additional paths with zero DDM due to reflections/structures; first at about twice the GP angle (6 deg for 3 deg); always above the true GP so not dangerous.

cards.q: ILS sensitivity?
cards.a: Localiser: full scale 2.5 deg, 0.5 deg per dot. Glide path: full scale 0.7 deg, 0.14 deg per dot. Max safe low deviation 2.5 dots (fly up).

cards.q: ILS identification?
cards.a: 4-letter Morse at 7 groups/min starting with I; suppressed if unserviceable; removed or continuous tone during maintenance.

cards.q: What is the ILS reference datum?
cards.a: A point about 50 ft above the intersection of runway centreline and threshold through which the extended glidepath passes.

cards.q: Significance of ILS X, Y, Z?
cards.a: Per ICAO Doc 8168, a suffix starting with Z is used when two or more procedures to the same runway cannot be distinguished by navaid type alone.

notes.b: Produces **360 radials** at 1 deg spacing, aligned to **magnetic north at the VOR site**. Frequency **108-117.95 MHz VHF**. Practically free of static and sky-wave interference, so usable day and night.
Receiver measures phase difference between two **30 Hz** signals: a **reference** (FM omni-directional) and a **variable** (AM, rotating pattern).

**BVOR**: broadcast VOR (weather/airfield info). **DVOR**: Doppler VOR, overcomes siting errors. **TVOR**: terminal, low power. **VOT**: test facility, broadcasts a fixed 360 deg test signal.
**DVOR difference**: reference signal is **AM**, variable signal is **FM**, and the directional signal rotates **anti-clockwise** to keep the same phase relationship. Less sensitive to site error.

1. **Site error** (terrain, buildings, trees, long grass).
2. **Propagation error** (terrain & distance - scalloping/bends).
3. **Scalloping**: imperfection in received signal making the CDI shift side to side.
4. **Airborne equipment error**.
Total error about **+/-5 deg**, plus pilotage error.
Airborne VOR parts: aerial, receiver, indicator.

cards.q: How does a VOR work?
cards.a: Phase comparison between a 30 Hz FM omnidirectional reference and a rotating 30 Hz AM variable signal; the phase difference gives the radial.

cards.q: Conventional VOR vs DVOR?
cards.a: Conventional: reference FM, variable AM. DVOR: reference AM, variable FM, rotating anti-clockwise; improves accuracy by being less sensitive to site error.

cards.q: Types of VOR?
cards.a: BVOR (broadcast), DVOR (Doppler), TVOR (terminal), VOT (test, 360 deg).

cards.q: VOR errors?
cards.a: Site, propagation (scalloping), airborne equipment; total about +/-5 deg plus pilotage.

cards.q: VOR frequency range?

notes.b:
**Primary**: reflected echo; Tx and Rx same frequency; single pulse; needs high peak power; weather-affected; depends on the target; no external help. Examples: **radio altimeter, GPWS, AWR**.
**Secondary**: ground interrogates, aircraft transponder replies; different frequencies; pulse pairs; less power; not affected by weather; independent of target reflection. Examples: **SSR, DME, TCAS**.
Primary gives better range/bearing but cannot identify aircraft individually.
Free from noise/static; short wavelengths give narrow beams, short pulses, and reflect efficiently from objects. Max theoretical range is set by **PRF**.

- **ASR**: area surveillance, 200-300 nm. **TAR**: medium range up to 75 nm for TMAs.
- **Aerodrome surveillance (approach) radar**: up to 25 nm, 3 cm or 10 cm; talk-down ends 2 nm from threshold.
- **PAR**: military only; 10 GHz (3 cm); azimuth + elevation (electronic glide path); ends at 1/2 nm or less.
- **ASMR/ASMI**: surface movement radar; 60 rpm, 15-17 GHz (SHF), 1.76-2 cm wavelength, 2.5-6 nm range.

Primary radar. Uses the **echo principle** for range and **searchlight principle** for bearing. Frequency about **9375 MHz** (+/-30), best returns from large droplets & wet hail in convective clouds. Uses: weather range/bearing, heaviest precipitation + turbulence, cloud height, ground mapping.
Colours: **Black** < 0.7 mm/hr; **Green** 0.7-4; **Yellow** 4-12; **Red** > 12 mm/hr; **Magenta** turbulence. Without magenta, red may flash red/black (cyclic).
Mapping: monochrome AWR, max 150 nm: **cosecant (fan) beam** for mapping to ~70 nm; **pencil beam** beyond.
Cloud height: tilt up until returns just disappear, then use 1 in 60. **Height ring** on older radars: vertical overspill showing roughly the aircraft's height; also means the equipment works. Height = (tilt - beamwidth/2) x range x 100 ft.

Ground interrogates on **1030 MHz**, replies **1090 MHz**. **Mode A** = identity, **Mode C** = altitude. Mode S = selective addressing; also used for TCAS.
Special codes: **7700** emergency, **7600** radio failure, **7500** unlawful interference (hijack), **2000** aircraft with no ATC instructions. Mode C operated with all codes.
4096 codes in Mode A (octal 4-digit). Problems: **garbling** (overlapping replies from aircraft within ~1.7 nm on the same bearing), **fruiting** (replies triggered by another interrogator).
**Mode S**: over **16.7 million** unique addresses (fixed to the airframe), data link (air-ground and air-air), fewer voice calls (via CDU), compatible with A & C.

cards.q: Primary vs secondary radar?
cards.a: Primary: echo of own pulse, no cooperation, high power, affected by weather (radalt, GPWS, AWR). Secondary: ground interrogation + transponder reply on different frequencies, pulse pairs, lower power, weather-independent, gives identity/altitude (SSR, DME, TCAS).

cards.q: SSR frequencies and modes?
cards.a: Interrogate 1030 MHz, reply 1090 MHz. Mode A identity, Mode C altitude, Mode S selective addressing/data link.

cards.q: Special SSR codes?
cards.a: 7700 emergency; 7600 radio failure; 7500 unlawful interference; 2000 no ATC instructions received.

cards.q: How many SSR codes in Mode A and Mode S?
cards.a: 4096 in Mode A; over 16.7 million in Mode S.

cards.q: Garbling and fruiting?
cards.a: Garbling: overlapping replies from aircraft on nearly the same bearing within ~1.7 nm. Fruiting: interference at an interrogator from replies triggered by another interrogator.

cards.q: AWR colours?
cards.a: Black <0.7, green 0.7-4, yellow 4-12, red >12 mm/hr, magenta = turbulence.

cards.q: How do you find storm cloud height on AWR?
cards.a: Tilt up until the returns just disappear and use the 1 in 60 rule (height = (tilt - beamwidth/2) x range x 100 ft).

cards.q: What's the AWR frequency and why?
cards.a: About 9375 MHz; best returns from large water droplets and wet hail in convective clouds.

cards.q: What is the height ring?
cards.a: Vertical overspill of beam energy reflected back that appears as a ring showing roughly aircraft height and confirming the radar is serviceable.

notes.b:
**Space** (24 SVs in 6 planes; 21 operational + 3 spares; altitude ~10 898 nm / 20 180 km; period 12 h; inclination 55 deg), **Control**, **User** (receivers).
Accuracy of the order of tens of metres. NAVSTAR (USA) and GLONASS (Russia).
Signals: **L1 1575.42 MHz** carries C/A code (repeats every ms), P code and nav message (50 Hz). **L2 1227.6 MHz** carries P code, used to determine **ionospheric delay**. Civilians use only **C/A** code; P is for military/approved users.

Ephemeris error (gravity, solar radiation); SV clock error (checked at least every 12 h); **ionospheric propagation error - most significant** (single frequency max ~5 m); tropospheric error (pressure, temperature, humidity, density).

**ABAS**: onboard integrity monitoring, e.g. **RAIM**. Needs **5 satellites** minimum for fault detection (the fifth detects the faulty SV).
**GBAS** (local area DGPS / LAAS): provides precision approaches by removing ephemeris and clock errors and minimising atmospheric errors; potential for **Cat IIIC**.
**SBAS** (wide area DGPS / WAAS): US WAAS operational July 2003; India's **GAGAN operational 2017**; also EGNOS.

cards.q: Describe the GPS segments.
cards.a: Space (24 SVs, 6 planes, 21 + 3 spares, ~20 180 km altitude, 12 h period, 55 deg inclination), control, user.

cards.q: GPS frequencies?
cards.a: L1 1575.42 MHz (C/A + P + nav message), L2 1227.6 MHz (P code, ionospheric delay), L3 1381.05 allocated for non-authorised users. Civil: C/A code only.

cards.q: GPS errors? The biggest one?
cards.a: Ephemeris, SV clock, ionospheric (most significant), tropospheric.

cards.q: What is RAIM and how many satellites?
cards.a: Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring - checks GPS integrity; needs at least five visible satellites for fault detection.

cards.q: ABAS vs GBAS vs SBAS?
cards.a: ABAS: onboard augmentation (e.g. RAIM). GBAS: local ground augmentation (LAAS) for precision approach, potentially Cat IIIC. SBAS: wide-area satellite augmentation (WAAS, EGNOS, GAGAN).

notes.b: Protects against malfunction/runaway by **limiting actuator authority**, so the pilot can always override.

Minimum **two independent autopilots**, **two independent radio altimeters**, and a **Cat III ILS** ground installation.
**Fail-passive**: a single failure doesn't endanger safety or cause big flight-path deviation, but the automatic landing capability is lost - pilot takes over. Needs **two** autopilots (duplex).
**Fail-operational**: after a failure (below alert height) the approach, flare and landing can still be completed automatically. Needs **three** (triplex).

Accurate height from **2500 ft to 0 ft**; uses **FMCW** (frequency modulated continuous wave). Errors: **fixed error** (indicator moves in 5 ft steps -> up to 2.5 ft discrepancy), and **mushing error** (different antenna heights relative to terrain).

Frequency lowered at night: electron density drops, signals travel higher before refracting and are refracted less -> a daytime frequency would give a **longer skip distance** and leave the receiver in dead space.

cards.q: Fail-passive vs fail-operational?
cards.a: Fail-passive: single failure leaves aircraft safe with no big deviation but can't complete autoland (two autopilots). Fail-operational: remaining system completes approach, flare and landing after failure below alert height (three autopilots).

cards.q: What does autoland require?
cards.a: Minimum two independent autopilots, two independent radio altimeters, Cat III ILS ground installation.

cards.q: How does a radio altimeter work and what are its errors?
cards.a: FMCW technique; accurate 2500 ft to 0. Fixed error (5 ft steps, 2.5 ft discrepancy) and mushing error (antenna height difference vs terrain).

cards.q: Why use lower HF frequencies at night?
cards.a: At night electron density decreases; signals go higher and refract less; a daytime frequency would give a longer skip distance and leave the receiver in dead space.
